## 3. What's new

- **Chemistry at rank 60 with full-XOR loaders.** somejoint's team pruned their R8 factorization to B = 143 vectors
  at rank C = 60 with 8-bit words, then refitted weights and offsets for the lowest λ_eff inside the error and gap
  limits. Every loader is now a full-XOR five-word lookup, and each low product is computed once. Within hours there were
  four variants on the same factorization, all re-verified by us:
  - [Atakan Aldemir, *C60 Reachable Cache*](https://www.kaggle.com/code/atakanaldemir/quantum-circuits-c60-reachable-cache), 3.4348 × 10⁸;
  - [Kirill Tymchishin, *Exact Gauge + 5-Word QROM*](https://www.kaggle.com/code/kirilltym/quantum-circuits-exact-gauge-5-word-qrom), 3.4481 × 10⁸;
  - [avazaku, *C60 Gauge Descent + Full-XOR QROM*](https://www.kaggle.com/code/avazaku/c60-gauge-descent-full-xor-qrom), 3.4496 × 10⁸;
  - [AlekseiProvorov, *Full-XOR Chemistry: No Borrowed Bits*](https://www.kaggle.com/code/leoprovorov/full-xor-chemistry-no-borrowed-bits), 3.4512 × 10⁸.
- **And then 22.70 (heliosli, version 12, late afternoon).** heliosli kept somejoint's factorization file byte for
  byte and five of its angle circuits, and rebuilt the other ten: 60 fewer Toffolis (16,366 → 16,306), chemistry
  cost −0.37%, best blend 22.70031 (re-verified by us).
- **889-qubit DQI from heliosli**, 1.8% cheaper than somejoint's 897-qubit decoder (re-verified by us). Comparing
  the two files, the change looks like a rearranged schedule for releasing and recomputing scratch registers. It removes
  8 qubits for only 30 more Toffolis, far below the roughly 1,100 Toffolis a qubit is worth at this size (our
  reading of the diff, not the author's description).
- **busyaprime's invsqrt** is mrmeows's 63-qubit circuit with one lookup re-synthesised from 186 to 172 Toffolis.
  The rest of the file is byte-identical to mrmeows's (we checked by diff), and the cost falls 0.85%.
- **Portfolios.** [alex chilton's *Verified Three-Task Portfolio*](https://www.kaggle.com/code/alexchilton/22-57-lb-verified-three-task-portfolio)
  scored 22.57358 on the board with the previous chemistry (observed). Its current version carries
  the 22.67 components. Its version table is the clearest record of who contributed what.
- **Audits and calculators.**
  - [ENES CAN (povaj1), *QCC Score Audit*](https://www.kaggle.com/code/povaj1/qcc-score-audit-local-vs-real-lb-scores)
    pairs six submissions' local reports with the scores they got (section 4 uses it).
  - [Harshit Kumar, *Marginal Value Calculator*](https://www.kaggle.com/code/harshitsama/quantum-circuits-marginal-value-calculator)
    ([753527](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/google-verifiable-quantum-circuit-compilation/discussion/753527)):
    removing one qubit is worth 1.6% of task cost on invsqrt and 0.23% on DQI and chemistry.
  - [Ak, *Reproducibility Audit*](https://www.kaggle.com/code/abisheksrivastav/quantum-circuit-portfolio-reproducibility-audit).
- **From source.** [Dmitrii Gluzdov, *Quantum Circuit Compilation from Source*](https://www.kaggle.com/code/dmitriigluzdov/quantum-circuit-compilation-from-source)
  builds its circuits from generators. That matters given the hosts' answer on prize eligibility in section 4.

## 4. From the forum

- **kickmix is on PyPI** ([753307](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/google-verifiable-quantum-circuit-compilation/discussion/753307),
  Tanuj Khattar, host): `pip install kickmix` now has prebuilt wheels for Windows, Linux and macOS (Apple Silicon
  and Intel), Python 3.10–3.14. This is the easiest way to verify locally.
- **Generators are required for prizes** ([752010](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/google-verifiable-quantum-circuit-compilation/discussion/752010)).
  Tanuj Khattar: "a circuit generator that produces the exact circuits must be provided", for all benchmarks and
  all prizes. Kaggle staff are confirming the details for reused upstream artifacts. The related question about
  reusing Apache-2.0 circuits ([753316](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/google-verifiable-quantum-circuit-compilation/discussion/753316))
  is still open.
- **Provenance of the frontier DQI.** Agniv Banerjee (somejoint) answered a question on
  [their notebook](https://www.kaggle.com/code/somejoint/quantum-circuits-22-67-local-gm-full-xor-chem/comments):
  all the DQI code in it was written by their team and is released under Apache 2.0, and earlier decoders are
  credited as design lineage only, implemented from a written description rather than from code. With
  heliosli's 889-qubit modification also Apache-2.0, today's public frontier is open-licensed throughout.
- **More measured nulls** ([753185](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/google-verifiable-quantum-circuit-compilation/discussion/753185),
  alex chilton). The chemistry Givens tree: re-encoding the same C46 vectors on 18 other trees and rounding to 8 bits,
  the starter tree rounds best. It reaches 219 mHa against 236 for a binary heap; relabelled orbitals are 17–29% worse,
  and chain or star trees are 80% worse. A staged round-and-refit on the best rivals is still running. He also points
  to the Eckart–Young floor we posted, R·C ≥ 290 for the 20 mHa gate, against 460–496 in public shapes (480 for
  today's best chemistry): room on paper, if anything can train there. On DQI, his list says peak-shaving the
  877-qubit build finds nothing under the exchange rate. heliosli's −8 qubits on the 897-qubit decoder suggests that
  build had slack the 877 didn't.
- **"What is the ceiling?"** ([753404](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/google-verifiable-quantum-circuit-compilation/discussion/753404)).
  Guesses range from 25 to 35. One reply notes that the pace has slowed since the first days, another that small
  randomness could decide near-ties. On that point:
- **The DQI score is a fixed draw per circuit, not per submission.** The verifier seeds every shot from
  SHA-256(circuit hash + salt) (`verify_submission_dqi.py`). The leaderboard numbers behave as if its salt is fixed:
  - Every pair of local report and board score we could find fits a whole number of hosted DQI failures to within
    0.00001: povaj1's six submissions, plus alex chilton's and busyaprime's shared 22.33981. busyaprime's notebook
    makes the same inference for its own entry.
  - The same circuit gets the same count every time, including across teams. The 897-qubit decoder drew 2 failures
    (−0.28%) for both teams that submitted it; locally it draws 0.
  - The 889-qubit decoder used by today's best portfolios draws 0 on the board, the best possible R.
  - A check on our own account: we predicted 22.70031 for today's best blend before submitting it, and the board
    returned 22.70030 (it shows five decimals).
  - So resubmitting the same circuit won't change its score. Any byte change re-rolls it, and final scoring uses a
    private salt, so the public draw tells you little about the final one
    ([753424](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/google-verifiable-quantum-circuit-compilation/discussion/753424)).

## 4b. Position risk: the final DQI draw, circuit by circuit

Final standings are rescored with a private salt. For DQI that is one fresh draw of failures for each circuit file,
and it can move a team's score by about 0.15% per failure. Two things follow from the verifier's design:

- **Identical files share a fate.** The seed is the file's hash plus the salt, so every team that submitted the same
  DQI bytes gets the same private draw. Copies of one portfolio rise or fall together; the risk is relative to teams
  with different DQI files.
- **A lucky public draw can only get worse.** A circuit showing 0 failures on the board can't improve at the final
  rescoring; one showing 2 probably will.

Per circuit, from our salt check (9 salts × 102,400 shots each, re-run daily; the leaderboard count is inferred
from board scores as in section 4). The failure rate behind each row is uncertain: for the frontier 889-qubit file
the 95% range gives P(worse) from 0.03 to 0.55.

| DQI file (SHA-256 prefix) | Qubits | Board failures | P(final worse) | P(final better) | Expected change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `4ee7a17b4cbc` (today's frontier) | 889 | 0 | 0.20 | 0 | −0.03% |
| `ef334fee63f3` | 883 | 0 | 0.28 | 0 | −0.05% |
| `7beea291a5de` | 889 | 0 | 0.63 | 0 | −0.14% |
| `f3d335c3f693` | 877 | 0 | 0.67 | 0 | −0.16% |
| `b3354f60e459` | 897 | 2 | ≈ 0 | 0.96 | +0.23% |

**What one failure is worth in rank.** On the 17:13 board, 97 teams sit within 0.153% (one extra DQI failure) below
the silver line, and 30 below the bronze line; the gold line has only 2 within reach. So around silver and bronze,
the final DQI draw can move a team by dozens of places. Teams whose DQI file differs from their neighbours' carry
that risk independently.

Our estimate, local re-verification; invsqrt and chemistry scores barely move with the salt. Tools: the
[DQI Salt Check](https://www.kaggle.com/code/manwithacat/dqi-salt-check-public-frontier) notebook measures every DQI
file in our dataset daily, so you can look up your own file by hash.

## 5. Tools and notes from us

- **[VQCC Apache-2.0 public circuits](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/manwithacat/vqcc-apache-public-circuits)**
  (dataset, Apache-2.0). It holds 60 DQI, invsqrt and chemistry circuits from public Apache-2.0 notebooks, with
  chemistry factorizations, de-duplicated by hash. Each entry has a credit and licence check and our local verifier
  score. Credit has two levels: the notebook that published the exact file, and, where we've compared files, who
  designed the circuit's core and what the publishing notebook changed. We add new circuits as they appear.
- **[The Real $150K Was the Friends We Made](https://www.kaggle.com/code/manwithacat/the-real-150k-was-the-friends-we-made).**
  It picks the cheapest verified circuit per task from that dataset, checks hashes, verifies, and writes a
  submission zip. It reruns whenever the dataset updates.
- **[DQI Salt Check](https://www.kaggle.com/code/manwithacat/dqi-salt-check-public-frontier)** re-measures the
  public DQI decoders under new salts each day.
- **ANGLE_k for every measurement outcome.** A formal check is
  [here](https://www.kaggle.com/code/manwithacat/prove-angle-k-for-every-measurement-outcome), with a technical
  note at [doi:10.5281/zenodo.23721373](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23721373).
- **Our kickmix fork: work in progress, more coming.**
  ([GitHub](https://github.com/manwithacat/kickmix-macos), Apache-2.0;
  [753230](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/google-verifiable-quantum-circuit-compilation/discussion/753230)).
  Faster and leaner local verification has been our side project this week. It isn't finished, and new features
  are on the way. Where it stands:
  - **Wins.** Results are identical to the official build on all three official verifiers. Large DQI circuits
    verify in a fraction of the memory. Today's release adds a batched phase read-out, which on a Mac makes a full
    invsqrt verification about 3.4× faster than the official build in our tests (the driver that uses it isn't
    published yet). Releases now mirror to Kaggle automatically as the
    [kickmix-fork-wheels](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/manwithacat/kickmix-fork-wheels) dataset, with a
    [kickmix_tools](https://www.kaggle.com/code/manwithacat/kickmix-tools) script to install and run it offline.
  - **Problems.** Speed doesn't carry over cleanly to Kaggle's Intel CPUs: in our invsqrt timings there, one circuit
    verified 1.6× faster and another 19% slower. The memory saving is the dependable part. With the official
    wheels now on PyPI, use those unless memory is your problem.
  - **Upstream.** One change is with the Qualtran maintainers: streaming `reaction_depth` instead of materialising
    every op ([PR #1994](https://github.com/quantumlib/Qualtran/pull/1994), for
    [issue #1993](https://github.com/quantumlib/Qualtran/issues/1993)). We'll offer more upstream if the maintainers
    want them, within their policy on AI-assisted contributions. All of this code was written with AI assistance.
- **Chemistry cold start on a T4 GPU: negative**, added to the null list in
  [753185](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/google-verifiable-quantum-circuit-compilation/discussion/753185).

- **How this gets made.** Every circuit in today's frontier table was pulled, hashed, licence-checked and re-verified
  by RezOps between 14:30 and 16:30 UTC. When a new one beat the old, the dataset was updated and the blend notebook
  re-ran on it. We're automating more of that loop. If you spot a credit or number that's wrong, say so
  in the comments: corrections go straight into the dataset.

## 6. What we think it means (opinion)

Today's public gain came almost entirely from chemistry, and on one shared factorization. DQI and invsqrt barely
moved. The top two teams are 13–15% above the public 22.70, a gap a single task can't easily close. With
generators now required for prizes, we'd expect more of the public work to become source rather than circuits. And
because the board's DQI draw is fixed per circuit, small public differences between near-identical portfolios
deserve less weight than they get.

Today's public gain came almost entirely from chemistry, and on one shared factorization. DQI and invsqrt barely moved. comments.rawMarkdown:
λ_eff hasn't moved much in public work (~48.7) while everything else has. 

Alex Chilton's nulls thread (https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/google-verifiable-quantum-circuit-compilation/discussion/753185) notes that every measured fit sits at Λ ≈ 290–308, and mrmeows (https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/google-verifiable-quantum-circuit-compilation/discussion/752757) showed that refits can't improve λ_eff by more than ~0.3% on a fixed factorization. Here's a complementary bound that holds for any factorization: with the official verifier's fixed symmetry shift, λ_eff can't go below ~46.8, about 4% under today's public value. The Λ > 49 floor in the task statement never binds.

**Setup** (notation as in the task paper and dfthc_math.py). The verifier fixes S and β₁. With w_B = W + s, where s = Σ_b w_b,

- Λ = λ_h1 + λ_h2, with λ_h1 = Σ|eig(h₁′)| and λ_h2 = ¼ Σ_{ρ,c} (Σ_b|w_b| + |W + s|)²
- E_gap = const + (λ_h1 − tr h₁′) + ½ ΣW², with const = E_upper − e_core + η β₁ (fixed)

**Step 1** (the gap floor forces the offsets). E_gap > 3.914898 requires 2·Σ(negative eigenvalues of h₁′) + ½ΣW² ≥ D := 3.914898 − const. For FeMoCo76o113e, const = −559.132, so D = 563.047 Ha.

**Step 2** (the triangle inequality). Σ_b|w_b| ≥ |s| and |s| + |W + s| ≥ |W|, so λ_h2 ≥ ¼ΣW².

**Step 3** (combine). Λ ≥ Σ(positive eigenvalues) + Σ(negative eigenvalues) + ¼ΣW² ≥ Σ(positive eigenvalues) + D/2 ≥ D/2 = 281.52 Ha. So at the gap floor, λ_eff = √(E_gap(2Λ − E_gap)) ≥ 46.79.

**Where the current public build stands**((8, 143, 60) 8-bit factorization by the SomeJoint team, with Dmitrii Gluzdov's gauge; official verifier formulas). I checked these numbers against the official verifier:

|   | Value |
| --- | --- |
|  Λ  | 304.82 (λ_h1 12.81 + λ_h2 292.01) |
|  ¼ΣW²  | 270.27 |
|  Bound D/2 + Σ(positive eigenvalues)  | 283.08 |
|  λ_eff now / lower bound  | 48.70 / 46.79–46.92 |


All of the remaining gap (21.7 Ha of Λ) is the triangle-inequality slack in λ_h2. Closing it would require every w_b in a (ρ, c) column to share one sign, with W aligned against s, while still fitting the two-body tensor within 20 mHa. Even closing it completely gains at most 3.9% on λ_eff, about +1.3% on the score. In practice the offsets W are already optimal: re-optimizing them alone with the floor enforced changes λ_eff by under 10⁻⁶ %.

**Takeaway:** chemistry gains have to come from T × Q (fewer addresses, narrower words, fewer copies), not from λ_eff.

Happy to be corrected if I've missed a degree of freedom. The derivation only uses the official verifier's definitions.

Most of what gets posted here is what worked.
Here is the other half: everything we tried that did not work, with the number that killed it.
If you were about to try one of these, this might save you a day.

All numbers are from the official verifiers or from our own exact re-implementations of their formulas, run locally.
The full table, with the source write-up for each row, is in the "What we tried that did not work" section of our notebook: https://www.kaggle.com/code/alexchilton/21-39-lb-verified-three-task-portfolio

## Chemistry (dfthcsos)

- **Re-rounding public 10-bit factorizations to 8 bits** (Özer's (32,60,30), (26,60,30), (24,60,30), marculera's (10,120,54), Gluzdov's word files): best error_2 162 to 201 mHa against the 20 mHa gate. The gate is set by how the words were trained, not by the weight count.
- **Fewer angle bits** (brot 7: error_2 349.7 mHa; brot 6: 794.5 mHa; brot 4: three orders over) and quantization-aware retraining on (40,60,30), (50,60,30), (55,60,30): every arm stuck at 30 to 40 mHa.
- **Lower Lambda with a different fit**: every fit anyone has measured sits at Lambda 290 to 308. A 2x would need 75.8.
- **Other J / lowbits on Rustad's (10,129,60) words**: J1, J2, J4 and J5 at lowbits 4 or 5 are all worse than J3. Our two-phase cache extended to J5 costs 508 Toffolis per circuit against a break-even of 401.
- **A linear change of the 11-bit address basis before the lookup**: the best layout reaches 266 products per circuit but needs 169 qubits (cap 128); every map whose cache fits is above 313. Streaming the high monomials over 2 to 6 measurement phases fits the cap but costs 350 to 974 Toffolis per circuit.
- **Rounding for the circuit, or reordering the Givens tree so consecutive word batches XOR to simpler tables**: on Özer's v9, the mixed (low x high) ANF matrix of every one of the 525 output bits has full GF(2) rank 15, exactly like a random matrix. His 321 Toffolis per circuit sit on the 262-product rank bound plus the caches. Saving one Toffoli would need an output's 85 columns to collapse into a 14-dimensional subspace. Column-pair XORs are 0.95 to 1.0x as complex as single columns, so reordering buys nothing either.
- **GPTQ-style rounding** (the LLM-quantization trick: round one angle at a time and correct the rest of the row in closed form from the Hessian): it does lower the error of each rounding step, but the refit after each stage absorbs it. From the same continuous start and schedule it ended at 47.04 mHa against 46.86 for a plain +-1 polish. What decides the result is the schedule (how finely you freeze and refit), not the per-row rounding rule.
- **One group fewer (R 10 -> 9) on the current best chemistry**: Özer's v9 is at error_2 19.998 mHa and E_gap 3.9151 (floor 3.915), and marculera measured nine merged groups at 22.1 mHa after rounding.
- **LLM-evolving the gauge optimiser** with ShinkaEvolve and a local Qwen 30B: 0 improvements in 15 generations. (Gemini in a hand-driven loop improved on its first try.)
- **Our gauge on Özer's v9 chemistry**: -0.0004 %. His lambda loop leaves nothing to rotate away.

## DQI

- **888 qubits from three source edits**: passes, but 4.7590e11 against 4.4860e11 at 889.
- **Dropping the jet zero flag**: 2 extra value errors on identical inputs, R 1.19126 -> 1.20139 (+0.85 %), against a qubit worth 0.225 %.
- **Freeing the constant-1 border word in the reverse folds**: 30 value errors, R +7.1 %.
- **Narrower reverse division**: +1,518 Toffolis (+0.32 %), more than the qubit is worth.
- **Porting the BM-decoder gadgets (Kozykorpesh, mrmeows q870) to the Schur decoder**: the structures they rely on do not exist there.
- **A cheaper inverse for the reverse extraction**: reverse costs 223 Toffolis per pair against 192 forward, and every route we found costs the same.
- **Peak shaving on Özer's 877-qubit build** (reorder, recompute, dirty or clean borrowing): with cost ~ Q^2 T, one qubit is worth about 1,100 Toffolis. The 877 peak is hit in 2,046 windows across about 684 kernel calls, there are 0 known-value qubits to borrow at the 1,734 jet windows, and the cheapest narrowing costs at least 23 to 42 Toffolis per window. So: nothing under the exchange rate.

## Inverse square root

- **Borrowing zero or affine-redundant wires, dropping degenerate Toffolis** (on our 66-qubit build and on the public 63): 0 degenerate controls in about 1,500 Toffolis, no borrowable wire in the rows.
- **Retuning or dropping the 44 rotation angles**: the LP gives the identical margin; dropping 1, 2 or 3 rotations gives worst error/tolerance 1.354, 2.214, 3.937.
- **Dropping one of the 32 Horner table bits and refitting**: every variant fails, the best at 1.228x the tolerance.
- **A dirty-wire AND for a row-opening gate**: the cheap cover (+23 Toffolis) is not valid, because the borrowed wires are read up to 8,474 times before the replay closes.
- **63 -> 62 qubits at all**: manwithacat's "Is the 63-qubit inverse square root optimal?" closes it far better than we did. Worth reading.

## Literature that did not give anything here

QROM halving (the chemistry QROAM cost is the verifier's formula, not our circuit), a GF(2^12) multiplier below rank 42 (only lower bounds exist), the reference DQI design in arXiv 2510.10967 (5.72e6 Toffolis), ECC repos and the MBUC gadget catalogue.

Credit to everyone whose public work made these tests possible: mrmeows, Agniv Banerjee (somejoint), Ahmed Berat Özer, Michael Rustad, marculera, heliosli, manwithacat, Kirill Tymchishin, Dmitrii Gluzdov, Kozykorpesh, jday96314 and the rest.

Great list, thank you. A few more from our side, in no particular order. Numbers are from the local official verifiers or exact local analysis unless stated, and the work was done with AI assistance.

**Chemistry** (details and the tools to check them in our [chemistry negative results notebook](https://www.kaggle.com/code/manwithacat/chemistry-negative-results-what-fails-and-why))
- Rounding a fixed 12-bit factorization uniformly to 11-bit angles: verifier FAIL at 76.9 / 29.7 mHa. Precision has to be co-fitted with the weights.
- Gauge and offset descent on public factors: H2_I gradient steps worsen cost in both directions (cusps at zero eigenvalues and zero weights); active-set projection 1.2e-5; pruning the weakest copy +0.29%; a fixed-word λ_eff refit −0.08%, decaying to about −0.13%. Consistent with mrmeows' ~0.5% bound.
- A smaller dictionary at R = 1 with 10–11-bit words, (1,460,384) and (1,496,300): 20.5–22.4 mHa continuous against the ~17 needed, with Gauss–Newton gaining ~1e-4 mHa per iteration after 3,764 iterations. Capacity, not the optimiser.
- Eckart–Young floors from the pair-space spectrum: R·C ≥ 290 for 20 mHa (307 for 15, 330 for 10). No shape below that passes however it's trained.
- A shared eigenbasis for the factors: pairwise commutators barely better than random (0.148 vs 0.161), joint diagonalisation moves off-diagonal mass only 17.6% → 16.4%, and a greedy eigen-dictionary sits at 1,279 mHa at B = 496.
- Dictionary-only search with an exact inner solve for the weights: public weights are within 0.5 mHa of optimal for their dictionary (19.466 vs 19.990), and dictionary-only L-BFGS loses to joint Gauss–Newton at equal wall clock (17.585 vs 17.072 mHa).

**DQI**
- Dropping the gap flag from the Berlekamp–Massey state: even restricted to syndromes of correctable errors, 24 post-step states collide between the two flag branches, so the flag carries information.
- Reusing the half-degree "Dialog" division in the reciprocal step: it divides modulo the wrong polynomial (E, where the map needs O² modulo σ = E² + zO²), so it can't be dropped in.
- A phase-only sweep with Newton/Hensel inversion: doesn't converge (classical test). The Fermat/Itoh–Tsujii replacement costs about 1.16 M Toffolis one way (formula, not built).
- Hunting cheap GF multiplications in a public 870-qubit BM decoder: 72.3% of its Toffolis are 16,998 GF multiplies (14,750 full 12-bit at 42 each), and there are no squares or constant/classical-factor products left: the designers already route those through CNOT-only operations.

**Inverse square root**
- Trading rotation precision where the error has slack: mapping error/tolerance over the whole input domain (with the verifier's own chunking and seeding) found no region with enough slack. The circuit is precision-saturated everywhere, so the rotation price can't move.

- Sampled "screening" doesn't beat the official verifiers on broken circuits. They already abort at the first failing chunk (a broken invsqrt candidate is refused in ~1.3 s), and DQI's ~1 s of load and hash is a floor.

- A straightforward bit-sliced GPU kernel (Metal, exact against kickmix): about the throughput of all 10 CPU cores of an M2 Pro (~5e11 op·shots/s), so no win on a laptop.
- Running verifier batches on threads with the GIL released: 2.7× for DQI but only ~1.2× for invsqrt, where per-shot Python work dominates. Separate processes are better.

  • Trading rotation precision where the error has slack: mapping error/tolerance over the whole input domain (with the verifier's own chunking and seeding) found no region with enough slack. The circuit is precision-saturated everywhere, so the rotation price can't move.

  • Sampled "screening" doesn't beat the official verifiers on broken circuits. They already abort at the first failing chunk (a broken invsqrt candidate is refused in ~1.3 s), and DQI's ~1 s of load and hash is a floor.
  • Simulating linear (X/CX/SWAP) blocks as GF(2) matrix products on tensor cores: only ~5% of DQI's ops, and none of invsqrt's or chemistry's, sit in blocks long enough to pay off.
  • A straightforward bit-sliced GPU kernel (Metal, exact against kickmix): about the throughput of all 10 CPU cores of an M2 Pro (~5e11 op·shots/s), so no win on a laptop.

comments.rawMarkdown:
This indicates that your decoder (or its uncomputation) is producing the wrong outcome on those rare inputs. 

When designing reversible quantum circuits, you have to make sure all ancilla scratch space is uncomputed. Doing an `HMR` on an ancilla qubit means you are shifting the uncomputation problem to the phase. `HMR` always resets the ancilla qubit to `|0>` (so `value_errors = 0`), and when the ancilla was `|1>`, you get a `-1` phase kickback whenever the measurement outcome is `1` (`H|1> = (|0> - |1>)/sqrt(2)`). If you don't uncompute the phase error correctly, you'll see 50% of the runs fail on the same input. Here is a minimal example to demonstrate the concept.

Suppose your input / output are four qubits `|q0>|q1>|q2>|q3>` and your goal is to apply the 4-controlled phase `(-1)^(q0 & q1 & q2 & q3) |q0>|q1>|q2>|q3>`. Since `kickmix` only has up to 2-control phase/Toffoli primitives (`Z`, `CZ`, `CCZ`, `CCX`), we compute `q0 & q1` into a scratch ancilla `q4`.
The reversible `kickmix` circuit uses **3 Toffolis** ([open in Quirk](https://algassert.com/quirk#circuit=%7B%22cols%22%3A%5B%5B%22H%22%2C%22H%22%2C%22H%22%2C%22H%22%5D%2C%5B%22Amps4%22%5D%2C%5B%5D%2C%5B%5D%2C%5B%5D%2C%5B%22%E2%80%A2%22%2C%22%E2%80%A2%22%2C1%2C1%2C%22X%22%5D%2C%5B1%2C1%2C%22%E2%80%A2%22%2C%22%E2%80%A2%22%2C%22Z%22%5D%2C%5B%22%E2%80%A2%22%2C%22%E2%80%A2%22%2C1%2C1%2C%22X%22%5D%2C%5B%22Amps4%22%5D%5D%7D)):
```text
CCX q0 q1 q4
CCZ q2 q3 q4
CCX q0 q1 q4
```
If you forget to include the last `CCX` that uncomputes `q4`, then you'd always see a value error on the 4 inputs on which `q0` and `q1` are both `1` ([open in Quirk](https://algassert.com/quirk#circuit=%7B%22cols%22%3A%5B%5B1%2C1%2C%22H%22%2C%22H%22%5D%2C%5B%22Amps4%22%5D%2C%5B%5D%2C%5B%5D%2C%5B%5D%2C%5B%22%E2%80%A2%22%2C%22%E2%80%A2%22%2C1%2C1%2C%22X%22%5D%2C%5B1%2C1%2C%22%E2%80%A2%22%2C%22%E2%80%A2%22%2C%22Z%22%5D%5D%2C%22init%22%3A%5B1%2C1%5D%7D)):
```text
CCX q0 q1 q4
CCZ q2 q3 q4
```

You can optimize the original circuit by replacing the uncomputing `CCX` with an `HMR` and a 0-Toffoli Clifford `CZ` phase correction ([open in Quirk](https://algassert.com/quirk#circuit=%7B%22cols%22%3A%5B%5B%22H%22%2C%22H%22%2C%22H%22%2C%22H%22%5D%2C%5B%22Amps4%22%5D%2C%5B%5D%2C%5B%5D%2C%5B%5D%2C%5B%22%E2%80%A2%22%2C%22%E2%80%A2%22%2C1%2C1%2C%22X%22%5D%2C%5B1%2C1%2C%22%E2%80%A2%22%2C%22%E2%80%A2%22%2C%22Z%22%5D%2C%5B1%2C1%2C1%2C1%2C%22H%22%5D%2C%5B1%2C1%2C1%2C1%2C%22Measure%22%5D%2C%5B%22%E2%80%A2%22%2C%22Z%22%2C1%2C1%2C%22%E2%80%A2%22%5D%2C%5B%22Amps4%22%5D%5D%7D)):
```text
CCX q0 q1 q4
CCZ q2 q3 q4
HMR q4 b0
CZ q0 q1 if b0
```
Now suppose you forgot the phase correction `CZ q0 q1 if b0` and instead ran ([open in Quirk](https://algassert.com/quirk#circuit=%7B%22cols%22%3A%5B%5B%22H%22%2C%22H%22%2C%22H%22%2C%22H%22%5D%2C%5B%22Amps4%22%5D%2C%5B%5D%2C%5B%5D%2C%5B%5D%2C%5B%22%E2%80%A2%22%2C%22%E2%80%A2%22%2C1%2C1%2C%22X%22%5D%2C%5B1%2C1%2C%22%E2%80%A2%22%2C%22%E2%80%A2%22%2C%22Z%22%5D%2C%5B1%2C1%2C1%2C1%2C%22H%22%5D%2C%5B1%2C1%2C1%2C1%2C%22Measure%22%5D%2C%5B%22Amps4%22%2C1%2C1%2C1%2C%22%E2%80%A2%22%5D%2C%5B%5D%2C%5B%5D%2C%5B%5D%2C%5B%22Amps4%22%2C1%2C1%2C1%2C%22%E2%97%A6%22%5D%5D%7D)):
```text
CCX q0 q1 q4
CCZ q2 q3 q4
HMR q4 b0
```
This circuit has zero value errors on every input (since `q0..q3` are untouched and `HMR` always resets `q4` to `|0>`). On the 4 inputs with `q0 & q1 = 1` (`|1100>`, `|1101>`, `|1110>`, `|1111>`), `q4 = 1` and applying an `HMR` causes a phase error 50% of the time, specifically whenever `HMR q4 b0` samples `b0 = 1` (you can also see those 4 amplitudes have wrong phase in the 4th quirk link whenever measurement outcome is 1).

Thank you - this is exactly the confirmation we were hoping for from the organisers, and the minimal Quirk example makes the mechanism unambiguous.

The equivalence you point at is the piece we had independently measured and can now name precisely. Running single- and double-HMR probes on |0> and |1> in kickmix, we found the phase kickback is

    phase ^= b & q      (b = classical outcome bit, q = ancilla value before HMR)

i.e. a Pauli-Z kicked back onto the control pattern exactly when the measured outcome is 1 - which is your `CZ q0 q1 if b0` line, generalised to whatever the ancilla was controlling. That rule reproduces both of your examples: with the correction the 4-input phase is exact; without it the four inputs with q0&q1=1 acquire a phase that depends on b0, hence the 50%-of-runs failure we observed for one special input (128/256 measurement streams wrong, 0/256 on inputs without the pattern).

Two things we would like your steer on, since they decide how much it is worth chasing to zero:

1. **Is R(eps+) driven purely by the measured residual rate eps+, or does the verifier also reward pe = 0 beyond that?** Our reading of the metric is that R is a fixed function of eps+, so a construction with pe = 0 and one with pe = 3 out of 102,400 differ by ~1.5% in final cost and nothing more. If that is right, the practical question is whether the ~1.6e-4 rare-input set can be enumerated and covered by explicit conditional corrections (classically-controlled Cliffords, zero Toffoli cost) rather than removed structurally.

2. **On the uncomputation accounting**: is a conditional CZ gated on an outcome bit billed at zero Toffoli, as our reading of the cost model says? If the full set of rare-branch corrections costs qubits/depth but no Toffoli, covering them seems almost free - and it would also answer whether the current frontier constructions (Q=889, T~474K, pe 0..4 across 20 salts) have room to both reach pe = 0 AND keep the tighter qubit budget, or whether those two goals trade off.

For context: our current dqi runs at Q=889 / T~474K with pe 0..4 depending on the salt, so the residual is already tiny in the eps+ sense; if the remaining gap is purely eps+-driven it is worth ~1% and we would rather spend the effort on peak qubits (which enter as Q^2). If instead there is a construction detail that makes pe exactly 0 at no cost, that is a different decision.

Happy to share the probe scripts (HMR semantics sweep + repeated-measurement-stream harness) if useful to anyone else hitting this.

We built a small viewer that runs mrmeows' 63-qubit invsqrt circuit (the 1,348-Toffoli build most of the frontier uses) in your browser, one input at a time: https://manwithacat.github.io/kickmix-macos/viewer/

Pick an x and watch its bits move through all 46,610 operations on 63 qubits: 17 stages from normalisation through the coefficient lookup, the arithmetic blocks, the 41 fine rotations and the long phase-repair tail. Lit bits are coloured by the phase so far, and a dial shows the phase closing in on 1/√x.

- **Play** runs the circuit start to finish (once, on a loop, or back and forth); **Sweep x** scrubs the input across its whole range so you can see where the circuit's behaviour changes. **Re-roll measurements** changes every mid-circuit measurement outcome; the middle shifts, the final phase doesn't.
- Tracks show Toffolis run, measurement-based clean-ups, branches skipped for this x, and which gates move the phase.
- **Precision across every x**: error ÷ tolerance for all 3,133,452 inputs (computed with kickmix). The worst is x = 161 at −0.99932; only 184 inputs are above 0.9 of tolerance and the mean is 0.21.
- **Qubits**: at most 35 of the 41 scratch qubits hold a 1 at any instant, yet all 41 are needed, because their lifetimes are staggered (shown as a background in the raster). Saving a qubit means re-packing lifetimes, not lowering a peak.
- **Load your own .kmx** to view your circuit the same way. It stays in your browser. It's a viewer, not a verifier.

The in-browser tracer matches kickmix exactly (all qubits, classical bits and the phase, on 2,299 inputs). Stage names are marked documented (from mrmeows' README and proofs) or inferred (read from the op stream), and the middle arithmetic stages are the least understood. If you spot something odd, or know what a stage is doing, please say so; that's half the point.

For fun, there's also a price tag: at rough 2026 numbers, running this "small" circuit with error correction needs about 48,000 physical qubits, around $2 billion of hardware, and about three weeks to do the verifier's 200 million shots. kickmix does the same check on a laptop in about 75 seconds.

The viewer is also in our kickmix fork (tools/circuit-viewer, https://github.com/manwithacat/kickmix-macos) if you'd rather run it locally.

comments.rawMarkdown:
The DQI decoders in the current public lineage (ours included) fail on a few inputs in every 100,000, by design. The rules allow this: the repetition factor R prices it, and it never fails a submission. But each DQI score is a random draw. The test inputs are seeded from the circuit's hash plus a salt, any change to the circuit re-rolls the public draw, and final scoring uses a private salt.

We measured the public DQI circuits under 9 salts each ([notebook](https://www.kaggle.com/code/manwithacat/dqi-salt-check-public-frontier)). The 877- and 889-qubit decoders fail on about 1 in 100,000 shots and draw zero failures only about a third of the time. The 883- and 897-qubit decoders fail on about 1 in 300,000, and a 1,893-qubit decoder never failed. The expected cost of a "lucky" zero-failure public draw is 0.05–0.16% of the overall score. Our own 22.00949 was such a draw; its expected score is about 21.998.

That's small, but if you're choosing final submissions between near-ties on public score, compare expected DQI cost rather than the observed one. The notebook runs weekly with the unchanged official verifier. Corrections welcome. (Done with AI assistance.)

A follow-up on *what* these rare DQI failures are, since we now have enough of them to look at.

We logged 47 failing shots across four public decoders (the 877-, 883-, 889- and 897-qubit circuits; 22 of them from 10.24M shots of the 897Q). All 47 behave the same way:

- They're deterministic in the input: replaying a failing input with fresh simulator seeds fails every time, and passing inputs never do. So they're properties of particular error patterns, not measurement luck.
- They're all phase errors. The syndrome and ancillas come back clean.
- Probing the circuit with single-bit masks shows which error word it "believed" it decoded. In every case that word has the right syndrome but shares none of the true error positions; it fills positions 0..69 exactly, occasionally plus a few extras.

Positions 0..69 are exactly the span of the classical-mask projection these decoders share (the 70-position Vandermonde term that subtracts the masks' known linear phase). Its contribution equals the phase of the unique word on positions 0..69 with that syndrome. So the simplest reading is that, on these rare inputs, the decoder finds no error positions (presumably an internal degenerate step, like a zero pivot), and what's left in the phase is just the projection's term.

That's a black-box reading; we haven't looked inside any decoder. If you're building or modifying one with the projection, flagging the "found nothing" case explicitly would at least make these failures visible and countable. The trigger rates differ between designs (roughly 1 in 100,000 to 1 in 500,000 shots), so it's worth measuring yours under several salts. Logs and probe scripts are on request. (Done with AI assistance.)

The score is a geometric mean, so 1% off any task's cost gives +0.336% on the score. But qubits are priced very differently:
- invsqrt (cost = Q x C, Q=63): one qubit = 1.61% of cost -> +0.54% score
- DQI (cost = R x Q^2 x T, Q=889): one qubit = 0.23% of cost -> +0.08% score
- chemistry (cost = lambda x T x Q, Q=430): one qubit = 0.23% -> +0.08% score
Cost-neutral trade rates from the public 22.63 table: about 26 Toffoli-equivalents per qubit in invsqrt, about 990 Toffolis per qubit in DQI.

With ratios of about 20x, 59x and 10x, the chemistry ratio is the lowest, so a new chemistry shape has the most room; DQI qubits are cheap to ignore, invsqrt qubits are worth 7x more.
